cf.title: Lazy LEFT NestLoop JOIN: gate rescanning of the inner side by outer-side-only join clauses
cf.authors: Andrei Lepikhov (lepikhov), Mikhail Zhilin (mizhka-at-pgpro), Peter Petrov (pspetrov)

input.subject: Do not scan index in right table if condition for left join evaluates to false using columns in left table

verdict_reasoning: The goal has shown demand, and the gating Result design follows what Tom Lane and Andres Freund suggested. Level 2 fails on open design points. prior-attempts-1: message #21 measures about 1500 ms against about 470 ms on master, and the planner makes no cost-based choice. standards-compat-1: a left join that returns rows on HEAD can raise division by zero, and the thread answers only with a link to a blog post. No reviewer has commented on opportunistic gating versus a cost-based path.

brief.title: Gate nested loop inner scan with outer-only left join clauses
brief.problem: In a nested loop left join, Postgres scans the inner side for every outer row, even when an ON clause that uses only outer columns is false. This hits ORM-generated polymorphic queries (Hibernate treat()) and sales schemas that left join product rows to per-category tables, and Andres Freund named psql and pg_dump catalog queries with the same pattern.
brief.proposed_design: The current patch puts a gating Result node with a One-Time Filter above the inner side of a nested loop. The filter holds the join clauses that reference only the outer relation, so the inner subtree runs only when they pass. The change is made at plan creation with no cost-based choice, adds a NestLoop flag 'keep_inner_rewind' so a Materialize on the inner side is not rescanned, and adds a second patch for pg_plan_advice.
user_visible_surface: EXPLAIN shows a new Result node with One-Time Filter on the inner side of a nested loop left join for outer-only ON clauses.
pg_plan_advice: a separate patch makes it look through gating Result nodes on the nested loop inner side.
Regression tests: patch 0001 adds a shared platform_independent_explain routine to mask platform-dependent EXPLAIN output.
author_claims: In the products/phones/vehicles example, each inner index scan runs about 5,000 times instead of 10,036.
A gated nested loop adds no noticeable overhead when rows pass the gate, so the author sees no need for a GUC or costing.
Worst case: an expensive gate with an empty inner side took about 1500 ms, against about 470 ms on master; overhead grows linearly with outer size.
v4 fixes wrong row counts with volatile clauses by following the qual_is_pushdown_safe rules.
The division-by-zero difference Bryan Green reported is a false positive, explained in the author's blog post.
brief.thread_state: Tom Lane and Andres Freund doubted in 2024 that the case is worth new mechanism, but suggested the gating Result approach the patch now uses. Since 2026 only Bryan Green has replied, reporting wrong results; v4 addresses the volatile cases, the division-by-zero case is disputed, and CFbot reports the patch needs a rebase.
unclear: The thread gives no reason in the thread itself why the division-by-zero error is acceptable; it points only to an external blog post.
The material does not say whether v4 still gates clauses that can raise errors or call stable functions.
No reviewer has commented on the opportunistic approach versus a cost-based GatingPath, which the author leaves open.
The brief has no commit message or documentation for v1 to v4, only for the 2024 prototype.
The material does not say whether the change applies to semi joins or only to left joins.
Planner cost estimates for the nested loop do not reflect the gate, and the material does not say whether this affects plan choice.

prior_attempts.title: Improve the performance of nested loop join in the case of partitioned inner table
prior_attempts.quote: In short, I think you're going to have to come up with something very crafty here to reduce the overhead worst case.
prior_attempts.reason: The author's own benchmark showed about a 4% slowdown when the parameter changes on every outer row, against about 20% gain when it stays the same. David Rowley judged that changed parameters are the common case and asked for a planner decision based on n_distinct or an executor heuristic, with the logic moved out of nodeNestloop.c. The author did not post an update, so the entry was returned with feedback.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 skipped partition pruning in nodeNestloop.c when parameters did not change; this patch adds a gating Result above the inner side. Both have a measured worst case and no planner decision.

objections.title: Unbounded worst-case cost with no planner choice to avoid it
objections.failure_scenario: A user runs a nested loop left join where the inner side is usually empty and the outer-only ON clause is expensive. After upgrade the gate runs on every outer row, and the query takes about three times longer. Nothing in the plan cost shows this, so the user finds out from production latency.
objections.argument: Message #21 measures about 1500 ms against about 470 ms on master and says the overhead is linear in outer size, with no ceiling. Yet v4 adds the gate at plan creation without costing. [P2] was returned for the same shape: a nestloop change with a worst-case slowdown and no planner or heuristic decision. Message #21 names the cost model as the open question, and message #19 notes a large footprint across regression test plans.
objections.author_must_show: How does the planner avoid the gated plan when the inner side is empty and the gate is expensive, and what does it cost to model?

precedents.title: Improve the performance of nested loop join in the case of partitioned inner table

critic.reasoning: Message #21 measures about 1500 ms against about 470 ms on master and leaves the cost model open. [P2] fits: a nested loop change with a measured worst case, where the reviewer asked for a planner decision.

objections.title: Left joins that return rows today can raise errors after upgrade
objections.failure_scenario: An application runs `o left join i on o.k = i.k and 1/o.x = 1` against a table where `i` has no matching rows. On HEAD it gets `(1, 0, NULL)`. After upgrading to a release with this patch, the same query fails with division by zero, and the user finds out in production.
objections.argument: Message #22 shows this with v3, and message #23 calls it a false positive without saying why in the thread. Postgres does not promise an order of clause evaluation, so a committer may accept that a qual now runs where it did not before. But this patch evaluates the clause for every outer row, including rows where HEAD never reaches the join qual, and the planner makes this change for every eligible plan without a cost choice. The thread does not say whether v4 still gates clauses that can raise errors.
objections.author_must_show: Does v4 still gate clauses that can raise errors, and what is the in-thread argument that turning working queries into errors after upgrade is acceptable?

critic.reasoning: Postgres does not promise a clause evaluation order, which weakens this objection. But message #23 answers the report only with a link to a blog post, and the thread does not say whether v4 still gates clauses that can raise errors.

objections.title: Always-on plan change with no way to turn it off
objections.failure_scenario: After an upgrade, a reporting query with an expensive outer-only ON clause and a mostly empty inner side runs about three times slower, as in message #21. The DBA cannot disable the gate per session and has to rewrite the generated SQL, which an ORM such as Hibernate may not allow.
objections.argument: The gate is added at plan creation with no costing, and message #14 rejects a GUC. Recent planner features such as Memoize came with an enable_* setting, so users have an escape hatch when the new shape loses. Message #21 measures the loss: no upper bound, linear in outer size times gate cost. Message #19 says the change has a large footprint in the regression tests. That means many existing EXPLAIN outputs change shape, which also affects extension tests and pg_plan_advice users.
objections.author_must_show: What can a user do after upgrade when the gated nested loop is slower for their query, without rewriting the SQL?

precedents.title: Improve the performance of nested loop join in the case of partitioned inner table

critic.reasoning: Message #14 rejects a GUC because of low overhead, but message #21 later measures a threefold slowdown, so the thread does not answer this. [P2] is not about an off switch and must not be used as support.

objections.title: Extra plan node forces changes in plan-shape consumers
objections.failure_scenario: An extension or contrib module that matches nestloop inner plan shapes, such as pg_plan_advice or a third-party hint module, meets an unexpected Result node after upgrade. Its plan checks fail or its advice stops applying. The maintainers find out from user reports.
objections.argument: Patch 0002 exists only so that pg_plan_advice can look through the new Result node. Messages #18 and #19 call that fix "quite a formal fix" and say the correct way to extend this machinery is not yet known. Each later change to plan shape would need the same fix in every consumer. The proposal does not say how external modules should detect a gating Result.
objections.author_must_show: How should pg_plan_advice and other plan-shape consumers recognize a gating Result in general, beyond the special case that patch 0002 adds?

critic.reasoning: Gating Result nodes already exist in plans, so the point about third-party modules applies to any plan-shape change. But message #19 calls the pg_plan_advice fix formal and says the correct way to extend it is not yet known.

refuted.title: Gate is applied without costing and has an unbounded worst case
refuted.failure_scenario: A user has a nested loop left join with an expensive outer-only ON clause and an inner side that usually finds no match. After upgrade, the clause runs once per outer row, and the query in message #21 goes from about 470 ms to about 1500 ms. The planner never weighs this, so no setting or plan choice avoids it.
refuted.argument: Message #21 says the overhead is linear in outer size times gate cost, with no ceiling. The cost model does not see the gate, yet the plan changes for every qualifying left nestloop, users and non-users of the pattern alike. In [P2], a nestloop optimization with a measured worst case was returned, and the reviewer asked for a planner-side decision. Message #19 argues the gate has no noticeable overhead, but message #21 contradicts that for the empty-inner case.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should the gate be applied without a cost check when message #21 shows a threefold slowdown that grows with outer size and is invisible to the planner?

precedents.title: Improve the performance of nested loop join in the case of partitioned inner table

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of prior-attempts-1. It has the same measurement, the same precedent and the same request for a cost-based choice.

refuted.title: New nestloop kind between parameterized and plain adds a silent trap
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch changes how nested loop sets REWIND or how Materialize decides to rescan, and does not account for keep_inner_rewind. Tests still pass, but the inner side of gated joins is rescanned on every outer row. Users notice only as a slowdown in production.
refuted.argument: Message #17 shows the first draft already hit this. The gating parameter made Materialize rescan its subtree 200 times, and only production-like tests found it. The fix is a flag derived from PATH_REQ_OUTER that future rescan and parameter code must keep consistent by hand. Nothing in the design makes a mismatch fail loudly. Message #17 itself calls this "a little different animal".
refuted.author_must_show: What check or test would fail if a future change to nestloop rescan or Materialize handling ignored keep_inner_rewind?

critic.reasoning: The scenario depends on an unnamed future patch and on the assumption that no test covers the rescan count. Message #17 shows the regression in EXPLAIN ANALYZE loop counts on regression tables, which a test can pin.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a NestLoop flag in plannodes.h, and a second patch makes pg_plan_advice look through the new Result node.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: The patch adds no GUC, and message #14 rejects one, so the always-on gate has no off switch.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: createplan.c adds a gating Result on the nested loop inner side for every eligible left join, without costing.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-1: Left joins that return rows today can raise errors after upgrade

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The keep_inner_rewind flag, the changed EXPLAIN output in many regression tests, and the pg_plan_advice patch all need upkeep.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The gate runs once per outer row in nodeNestloop.c; message #21 measures about 1500 ms against about 470 ms.

questions: How does the planner avoid the gated plan when the inner side is usually empty and the outer-only clause is expensive?
Does v4 still gate clauses that can raise errors, such as `1/o.x = 1`, and what is the in-thread argument that the new error is acceptable?
What can a user do after upgrade when the gated nested loop is slower for a query that an ORM generates and that cannot be rewritten?
Why is gating at plan creation better than a cost-based GatingPath, given that nested loop cost estimates do not reflect the gate?
How should pg_plan_advice and other plan-shape consumers recognize a gating Result in general, beyond the special case in patch 0002?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the planner's outer join clause placement and the nested loop rescan and Materialize code. Tom Lane and Andres Freund commented in 2024, but nobody of that kind has reviewed v1 to v4.
committability.liability: The owner signs for wrong-result and new-error reports on left joins, for plan regressions with expensive outer-only clauses, and for keeping keep_inner_rewind consistent with later rescan changes, with no end date.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v4 to fix the wrong row counts that Bryan Green reported and moved the entry to the next CommitFest in October 2026. CFbot has reported a pending rebase since 2026-10-20.

priority.reason: Hibernate treat() queries, a sales-schema request, and psql and pg_dump catalog queries show the pattern is common. The costing question and the new-error question are open, and the change touches the planner, the executor and many regression test plans.

provisional_note: The v4 code was not read. I could not check which clauses v4 gates (error-raising, stable or non-leakproof), whether semi joins are affected, or how keep_inner_rewind interacts with Materialize rescans.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: prefetching for nestloop / indexscan
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds an ExecPrefetch executor callback so that a nested loop reads a batch of outer rows and asks a parameterized inner index scan to prefetch the matching heap pages. It is a small proof of concept limited to nestloop with an inner index scan, controlled by a new enable_nestloop_prefetch setting.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the entry because the patch was a quick experiment and he had no time to keep working on it. Before that, Andres Freund questioned the extra executor tree traversals and suggested passing multiple values down in one parameter, possibly as one ScalarArrayOps index scan. Peter Geoghegan supported that direction. The author agreed it looks like block nested loop join, which moves the work away from this design, and his cached-data benchmark showed about a 30% regression.

precedents_retrieved.title: [PATCH] Equivalence Class Filters
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds equivalence filters to equivalence classes, so a btree-operator clause of the form "Expr op Const", such as t1.id <= 10, is also applied to the other members of the class, such as t2.id. The planner collects these clauses while it builds the equivalence classes, then attaches each one to the class that contains its expression.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane said the matching search would cost planner cycles on every query, often for no gain, and that redundant derived clauses could skew selectivity estimates. Robert Haas showed that pushing the inequality to every relation can make execution slower, for example a retest on the inner side of a parameterized nested loop, and that choosing where to apply it is hard. David Rowley then said the patch was not wanted in its current form and that he would not work on it further.

precedents_retrieved.title: INNER JOIN removals
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch uses foreign key constraints to remove semi, anti and inner joins whose result is already guaranteed by the constraint. Because pending foreign key triggers can make such a removal wrong, the later versions plan the join normally and prune the unneeded join nodes at executor start-up when the trigger queue is empty.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author marked this entry rejected because it had become a duplicate. He had moved the patch to a new thread and a newer commitfest entry, where he said it was ready for review. Before that, Michael Paquier had proposed rejecting it because the last version still had FIXMEs and had seen no activity for months. The visible messages show no rejection of the design itself.

precedents_retrieved.title: Table Partition + Join Pushdown
precedents_retrieved.summary: When a hash join has a partitioned (inheritance) table on one side, the planner would push the join below the Append, joining each child separately. Each child's CHECK constraint is rewritten through the join clause into a filter on the other relation, so each per-child hash table holds fewer rows.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas pointed out that a CHECK(P(x)) constraint on A does not mean that only rows with P(y) true can join when A.x = B.y, because equality under the join operator need not mean equality for all purposes. For numeric, 1 and 1.0 are equal but differ under length(x::text), so the derived filter can drop matching rows. He said the whole patch rests on this idea, and suggested hash partitioning with the opclass hash function as the safe way to get the same optimization.

precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The fundamental problem is that equality according to the join
operator need not mean equality for all purposes.  1 and 1.0, as
numerics, are equal, but not the same.

precedents_retrieved.title: hash joins with bloom filters
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch builds a Bloom filter over the inner side of a hash join and checks outer tuples against it before the hash table probe or before writing them to a batch file. Filter sizing uses estimated row counts or 1/8 of work_mem, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports filter statistics.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped working on it and asked for it to be marked returned with feedback; no one took it over. He said pushing the filter down to the outer scan would make it more useful, but he had no clear plan for that. Robert Haas noted that costing it well enough to avoid regressions looks hard.

precedents_retrieved.title: INNER JOIN removals
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner remove an inner-joined relation when none of its columns are used and a foreign key proves a matching row exists. Because pending foreign-key triggers can break that proof at run time, the planner builds two plans, one with the joins removed and one without, and an AlternativePlan node picks one at executor startup.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected to the design, the risk of bugs and the cost. The AlternativePlan node breaks the one-to-one match between plan trees and planstate trees, and calling make_one_rel() twice is unreliable because the planner changes its input data structures. He also doubted that "no pending AFTER trigger events" proves the foreign keys hold for the snapshot in use, and he noted new O(N^2) planning work and a pg_constraint lookup for every scanned relation.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent is the same idea. The thread's own 2024 discussion (messages #3, #4, #7) doubted demand but proposed the gating Result design that the patch now follows.
Two objections from the standards and compatibility angle. The proposal adds no SQL syntax, catalog objects or pg_dump changes, so those touch points are clear.

The proposal changes only plan shape and executor behaviour inside one backend: a gating Result node and a NestLoop flag. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog column, wire protocol message or replicated state. The plan node struct change goes only into a new major version and is not backpatched, so no stable ABI is affected. Effects on plan-walking extensions such as pg_plan_advice belong to other angles.

I found no privilege or exposure aspect, so I raise no objections from the security angle. The patch adds no object, privilege, GUC, function or catalog entry. The gating Result runs on the inner side, after the outer scan has already applied its RLS and security barrier quals, so the gate's outer-only clause sees only rows the user can already read. It cannot see inner data, so it cannot leak inner rows past inner-side RLS. Bryan Green audited v3 for security in message #22 and reported only correctness differences. The extra error in that report (division by zero) and the volatile-clause row counts are correctness issues, and the slowdown with an expensive gate is a performance issue; other angles cover these. Without the code I cannot check whether v4 still evaluates leaky or non-leakproof clauses on rows the old plan never reached.
Three objections are raised from the maintenance and fit angle.

Postgres has no existing feature that skips the inner scan of a nested loop left join for outer-only ON clauses in generated SQL. A hand-written lateral subquery fenced with OFFSET 0 can likely get a one-time filter, but the Hibernate treat() queries in message #5 cannot be rewritten, and no known extension does this.

The thread shows demand from three independent sources: Hibernate treat() queries (message #5), a sales-schema user request (message #8), and Postgres's own psql and pg_dump catalog queries (message #6). ORM-generated SQL cannot easily be rewritten, and the gate's cost falls only on queries that use the pattern, so I see no demand objection. Production numbers would still help the cost-model debate.
